Conquering the Scottish Highlands

The Scottish Highlands are the ultimate UK motorcycle touring destination. Vast empty landscapes, dramatic mountain passes, remote single-track roads, and a sense of wilderness unmatched anywhere else in Britain. But the Highlands also present unique challenges that your bike choice must address.

Highland Riding Challenges

Roads in the Highlands range from smooth dual carriageways to rutted single-track with passing places. Fuel stations can be 60-80 miles apart in the most remote areas. Weather changes rapidly — four seasons in one day is the Highland norm. Wind exposure on coastal and mountain roads can be extreme, and rain is measured in days rather than showers.

What Your Highland Bike Needs

  • Fuel range — At least 200 miles from a full tank. Running dry in the remote Highlands with no mobile signal is a genuine risk.
  • Manageable weight — Single-track roads require confidence and occasionally reversing. Lighter bikes are less stressful.
  • Wind protection — Exposed coastal roads and mountain passes mean sustained crosswinds. A good fairing and screen reduce fatigue.
  • Reliability — Breaking down 50 miles from the nearest village with no phone signal demands a bike you can trust absolutely.

Best Highland Touring Bikes

BMW R 1300 GS — The complete Highland package. Massive fuel range, outstanding weather protection, electronic suspension for variable surfaces, and BMW dealer support at Inverness and Fort William.

Triumph Tiger 1200 Rally Pro — Shaft drive, big fuel tank, and that wonderful triple engine. Handles everything from the A9 to the most remote single-track with confidence and character.

Yamaha Tenere 700 — The lightweight option for riders who prefer agility over luxury. The fuel range is more limited but the riding experience on Highland single-track is sublime.

Honda Africa Twin CRF1100L — Honda reliability in the most remote setting. The DCT automatic version removes clutch fatigue on endless stop-start single-track. Adventure-ready for any surface.

Kawasaki Versys 1000 SE — Outstanding motorway comfort for the long ride north, with electronic suspension that adapts to Highland B-roads. The inline four's smoothness reduces fatigue over long days.

Always fill up when you see a fuel station in the Highlands, regardless of how much fuel you have. The next one might be 70 miles away, and it might be closed when you get there. Fuel anxiety ruins Highland touring enjoyment.

Planning Your Highland Tour

Allow more time than you think. Highland roads are slow — average speeds of 35-40mph are realistic on single-track sections. Ferries to islands require advance booking in summer. Book accommodation ahead during July and August when capacity is stretched across the Highlands. Read our Best Motorcycles for the NC500 in Scotland guide for more. faq.q: How much fuel range do I need in the Highlands?
faq.a: Aim for at least 200 miles from a full tank, as fuel stations can be 60-80 miles apart in the most remote areas and running dry with no mobile signal is a genuine risk. Always fill up when you see a station, because the next one might be 70 miles away and closed.

faq.q: What is the best bike for Highland touring?
faq.a: The BMW R 1300 GS is the complete package, with massive fuel range, outstanding weather protection, electronic suspension for variable surfaces and dealer support at Inverness and Fort William. The Triumph Tiger 1200 is a superb alternative with shaft drive and a big tank.

faq.q: Is a lightweight bike viable up there?
faq.a: Yes, if you value agility over luxury. The Yamaha Tenere 700 is sublime on Highland single-track and easy to manage when reversing on narrow roads, though its fuel range is more limited, so plan fuel stops carefully and top up at every opportunity in remote areas.

faq.q: How should I plan a Highland tour?
faq.a: Allow more time than you think, as average speeds of 35-40mph are realistic on single-track sections. Book island ferries in advance during summer and reserve accommodation ahead in July and August when capacity across the Highlands is stretched. Reliability and wind protection are key.
